draft.title: Double entry accounting
card: Every transaction affects at least two accounts. A business records each one with at least one debit and at least one credit.
The total of the debits must equal the total of the credits for every transaction. The two sides are always equal in value.
Some transactions have more than two parts. A sale of goods might be recorded with one debit and two credits, as long as the debit total equals the credit total.
Because each transaction is balanced, the ledger as a whole stays in balance. Recording only one side would break this.
draft.remember: Every transaction needs debits and credits of equal total value.

a.q: Why does double entry accounting keep the ledger in balance?
opts: Each transaction has debits and credits of equal total value
Each transaction is recorded in only one account at a time
Each account is made to finish the period with no balance
The owner checks each transaction before it is entered
a.why: Every transaction is recorded with debits equal to credits, so adding it never upsets the balance. Recording in one account only would break the balance, not keep it.
a.clue: Think about the two sides of each single transaction.

b.q: Mia's Bikes in Geelong records a sale with a debit of $300 to Cash and a credit of $200 to Sales. What is needed for the entry to follow double entry?
opts: Nothing, as the entry is already complete
b.why: Debits are $300 but credits are only $200. A further credit of $100 in total is needed so both sides equal $300. Adding a debit would widen the gap.

a.best: Each transaction has debits and credits of equal total value
